original_value: Applicable and accurate assessment methods are required for a clinically relevant quantification of habitual physical activity (PA) levels and sedentariness in older adults. The aim of this study is to compare habitual PA and sedentariness, as assessed with (1) a wrist-worn actigraph, (2) a hybrid motion sensor attached to the lower back, and (3) a self-estimation based on a questionnaire. Over the course of one week, PA of 58 community-dwelling subjectively healthy older adults was recorded. The results indicate that actigraphy overestimates the PA levels in older adults, whereas sedentariness is underestimated when compared to the hybrid motion sensor approach. Significantly longer durations (hh:mm/day) for all PA intensities were assessed with the actigraph (light: 04:19; moderate to vigorous: 05:08) when compared to the durations (hh:mm/day) that were assessed with the hybrid motion sensor (light: 01:24; moderate to vigorous: 02:21) and the self-estimated durations (hh:mm/day) (light: 02:33; moderate to vigorous: 03:04). Actigraphy-assessed durations of sedentariness (14:32 hh:mm/day) were significantly shorter when compared to the durations assessed with the hybrid motion sensor (20:15 hh:mm/day). Self-estimated duration of light intensity was significantly shorter when compared to the results of the hybrid motion sensor. The results of the present study highlight the importance of an accurate quantification of habitual PA levels and sedentariness in older adults. The use of hybrid motion sensors can offer important insights into the PA levels and PA types (e.g., sitting, lying) and it can increase the knowledge about mobility-related PA and patterns of sedentariness, while actigraphy appears to be not recommendable for this purpose.

result.paraphrase: Accurate, suitable assessment methods are needed to quantify habitual physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior in older adults in a clinically meaningful way. This study set out to compare habitual PA and sedentariness measured by (1) a wrist-worn actigraph, (2) a hybrid motion sensor placed on the lower back, and (3) questionnaire-based self-estimation. PA was monitored for one week in 58 community-dwelling, subjectively healthy older adults. The findings show that actigraphy overestimates PA in older adults and underestimates sedentariness relative to the hybrid motion sensor method. Significantly longer daily durations (hh:mm/day) for all PA intensities were recorded with the actigraph (light: 04:19; moderate to vigorous: 05:08) than with the hybrid motion sensor (light: 01:24; moderate to vigorous: 02:21) and self-estimated durations (light: 02:33; moderate to vigorous: 03:04). Actigraphy-based sedentariness durations (14:32 hh:mm/day) were significantly shorter than those measured with the hybrid motion sensor (20:15 hh:mm/day). The self-estimated light-intensity duration was also significantly shorter than the hybrid motion sensor result. Overall, the study underscores the importance of precise quantification of habitual PA and sedentariness in older adults. Hybrid motion sensors can provide valuable insight into PA levels and PA types (e.g., sitting, lying) and improve understanding of mobility-related PA and sedentary patterns, whereas actigraphy does not appear suitable for this purpose.
